name: 4-Androstenediol (4-AD)

lead: 4-Androstenediol is a steroid closely related to testosterone that was sold as an oral supplement in the 2000s, with claims it would raise testosterone and build muscle.
No controlled trial of it for physique goals turned up. Reviews of the wider prohormone class describe the marketing claims as poorly supported.

paras: It is reported to convert to testosterone in the body at a modest rate, partly via a different enzyme pathway than androstenedione, and some of the resulting testosterone can convert to estrogen. In vitro data show testis tissue can make the conversion.
Reviews of oral andro prohormones raised concerns about health risks, and related 19-nor prohormones are on the WADA prohibited list. Specific legal status was not documented in the sources reviewed.

lead: 4-Androstenediol (androst-4-ene-3β,17β-diol, often abbreviated 4-AD or 4-diol) is an androgen-related steroid that was sold in the early 2000s as an oral "prohormone" dietary supplement, marketed to raise testosterone and support muscle growth.[1][2] It is a close chemical relative of testosterone and is described as converting to testosterone in the body at a low rate.[1]

Laboratory work shows that rat testis tissue can convert 4-androstenediol to testosterone in vitro,[3] and the compound has been studied mainly in the context of doping detection, where urinary markers have been developed to identify its administration in athletes.[4] A review of the broader "andro" prohormone class concluded that marketing claims of increased testosterone, strength and muscle mass had not been well supported by controlled human studies and that potential health risks were a concern.[2]
No clinical trial of 4-androstenediol for appearance or physique goals was found in the sources reviewed.
infobox: 1999 patent held by Patrick Arnold for raising testosterone[1]

paras: Wikipedia reports that 4-androstenediol converts to testosterone at roughly 16 percent, about three times the rate reported for androstenedione, through a different enzymatic route, and that some downstream testosterone is converted to estrogens.[1] The same article describes it as a weak partial agonist of the androgen receptor that can behave like an antiandrogen when full agonists are present, and as only very weakly estrogenic.[1]
A 1966 in vitro study found that rat testis tissue converted both 4-androstenediol and 5-androstenediol to testosterone.[3]

In the late 1990s and 2000s a group of oral products containing androstenedione, 4-androstenediol, 5-androstenediol and 19-nor analogues was marketed to the general public with claims of higher testosterone, strength, muscle mass, reduced body fat, better mood and sexual function.[2] Wikipedia notes a 1999 patent held by Patrick Arnold on using 4-androstenediol to raise testosterone in humans.[1]

Related 19-nor compounds such as 19-nor-4-androstenediol are on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list, and analytical papers describe urinary metabolite profiles used to detect them.[5] A forensic study examined urinary markers for identifying 4-androstenediol administration in athletes.[4]

No studies found. A review of the wider class of oral andro prohormones examined whether the potential risks outweighed the benefits and questioned the marketed claims.[2] Animal research on a related compound, 19-nor-4-androstenediol-3β,17β-diol, reported selective stimulation of muscle and bone relative to prostate in rats, but that is a different molecule and not a human study.[6]
